photographs.prompt:
Edit the FIRST input photograph. One full-bleed photographic image, wide 2.098:1, same camera and composition for a print gardening book. INPUT 1 is the base photograph for this exact first step. INPUT 2 is a three-view contact sheet of REAL CAMERA photographs of the man in the scene: very important for reshaping his jaw and chin faithfully. INPUT 3 supplies his actual cool-weather clothing only. This is one Cornish late-autumn afternoon, outdoors after a light shower, with cool overcast soft grey light, slight damp sheen on a few leaves and the tarp but no pouring rain or puddles. The picture will be paired with a warm sunny view taken the following late spring.
Keep John kneeling on the grass on the right, lowering the final brick onto the near right hem of a flat fully opaque, ordinary dark forest-green woven tarpaulin. Match his two hands on the brick, the ordinary perimeter weights, the existing layout and perspective of the tarp, his charcoal jumper, dark blue jeans and work shoes. Keep the fence, its worn low wall and the tiny slice at far right of his glass greenhouse on a pale grey brick plinth. Same understated, matter-of-fact photograph with comfortable headroom. NO shed.
The owner asks for a proper established lawn. REPLACE ALL the sparse, coarse and muddy ground visible OUTSIDE the edges of the tarp and under the actor with dense, closed, lush short mown lawn, attractive but authentic Cornish grass, mixed fine blades close together. A living continuous carpet with no earth peeking through it, right up to the tarpaulin, visible in front, along each side and behind. A few discreet recognisable flat dandelion, clover or plantain rosettes growing low in that lawn, especially near a tarp corner, testify to the weedy area, not an overgrown meadow. Leave the cover intact, flat and fully covering the treatment area with no dead weeds arranged on it. Subtle late-autumn clues only e.g. a couple of small fallen leaves at the fence, subdued greens; don't drown the details or darken the face.
Correct John's likeness using the real close views in the SECOND input as the authority. Match the slimmer taper in his lower cheeks, the small softly rounded and slightly set-back chin, his short mixed grey beard following his skin, softer natural jaw-to-neck transition. In particular bring back the protruding lower outline relative to the lower lip seen in the base, so it doesn't jut forward, square off, or appear reinforced by a shadow or by a thick block of beard. A relaxed mature man concentrating on the brick, still the same John, his natural forehead, hairline, nose and expression. Keep the downward gaze but let sufficient three-quarter part profile be seen to read the actual jaw contour. Understated documentary realism, normal texture, one image only, no typography or collage.

Make a single documentary garden photograph at a NEW, slightly oblique camera angle, wide 2.10:1 landscape for a practical printed gardening book. Reference 1 is the prior spring shot of the same place and John. Its arrangement of dead leaves and weeds is visibly staged and WRONG: replace the ENTIRE surface of the tarped patch with what a real lawn looks like after an opaque tarp has lain tight over short-mown grass and weeds through a damp winter. Use naturalistic observation from field photographs immediately after lifting an opaque lawn cover: irregular mottling of dark exposed soil and earth-stained brown plant remains, much of the foliage gone. A fine, almost two-dimensional layer of decomposing grass, a patchy short silky/tangled felt of fine blades in dirty beige, warm grey-brown and near-black, pressed into the soil where it grew, some portions barely distinguishable from the earth. No garden debris has been brought onto this patch. Show traces of a few small collapsed lawn weeds interwoven with the grass, at natural lawn scale: partly rotted threadlike branching runners, a few indistinct dark crumpled fragments still attached near their crowns. The dead roots and turf form one continuous skin that thins in places. It must NOT read as dozens of individual motifs scattered around a brown surface or big dandelion leaves laid down over dirt. The reference photo's intact pale rosettes, individual big pale leaves, branched twigs, and arranged heap should be altogether gone. No whole detached weed plants, no hay, straw mulch, or autumn tree leaves.
Catch ONE moment midway through a rake stroke. The rake teeth are in the felt, teasing up a small uneven ragged lip of the SAME fine grass mat, narrow and dark, with damp soil in the fibres and strands trailing back into the unworked surface. It has modest relief of 2–4 centimetres where the teeth pucker it. In front of the teeth lies undisturbed flat discoloured turf, with irregular earth showing through; behind the teeth toward the gardener a short darker combed strip and faint tooth marks show the actual direction of pull. It is a bed being cleared, not a pile of weeds being collected. The rest of the grass outside the rectangle is full, short, dense living green lawn.
The photographer returned several months later on a sunny late-spring day. REPOSITION the actual camera: take a step (about 0.7–0.9 metre) to the LEFT of the first camera and lower the camera around 20–30 cm, aim diagonally back to the RIGHT across the near-left corner of the patch at John's working hands. A visibly fresh perspective: the bed's long edge, low wall and rear fence recede at a gentle diagonal rather than dead horizontal, the folded tarp is offset by parallax, closer tufts slightly larger. Genuine 3-D parallax, horizon level, no simple roll or rotating the original. Keep the fence and its weathered pale masonry wall, rear-left folded tarp and weights, and only a thin glimpse of the greenhouse on its brick plinth at far right; camera still closely on action. Ref 3 is real ground reference for greenhouse structure only. No blue shed. No extra garden. John works from the grass on the right, three-quarter working profile, naturally forward slightly looking down at the teeth, recognisable in olive T-shirt and olive shorts with brown shoes in reference 1. Reference 2 shows his actual face and slight soft rounded chin in side and front view; follow the real softer chin and short grey beard. Real single wooden-shaft soil rake with right-angle metal head teeth downward, held in both hands; strong visual connection rake–felt–combed ground. Normal UK late spring sun with consistent soft-edged cast shadows and natural green. Keep face, rake, patch and small greenhouse clue in frame. This should feel like a candid photograph on a different day, not a duplicate take or composited items. Full bleed colour, one photograph only.

visual_research.source: University of Minnesota Turfgrass Science, Gary Deters, Figure 3
visual_research.observation: Direct lawn example after removing an opaque tarp: bare ground mixed with brown vegetation in irregular low patches. Some violets survived in this trial.

visual_research.source: Winterizing Garden Beds, Tarping to Reduce Tillage, p. 8
visual_research.observation: Three-frame bed sequence showing brown residual growth and exposed soil as the cover is pulled back.
